commentary:
Risk appetite firmed overnight, and energy is the story: crude extended its retreat, with Brent down 2.4% to $103 and WTI back toward $100, distillates leading the slide (heating oil -3.2%, gasoil -2.7%) — striking given a Saudi pipeline outage and ongoing Strait of Hormuz disruption hitting a market already short of buffers. That pullback in the inflation input matters most a day after the Fed, under Chair Warsh, delivered its first hike since 2023 and signalled another to come: falling oil bolstered the view that inflation can be contained without an aggressive cycle, letting stocks and Treasuries rally together.

Nasdaq futures gained 1.1%, the long bond firmed 0.4%, and the dollar eased from its peak even as Trump blasted a "hostile" Fed board. The central-bank picture stays hawkish at the margin. Jobless claims at their lowest since mid-May keep the Fed's case intact, while the BoE held at 3.75% in a 6-3 vote, with Bailey warning policy may have to tighten if the Middle East conflict is prolonged, and unveiled a full APF unwind — £368bn of gilt stock gone by end-2034 — though gilts still caught the oil-led bid. The BoJ is next, expected to hike to a 31-year high, so watch yen and JGB-linked flows.

China trimming its Treasury holdings to a 2008 low is a longer-run caveat for the US long end. Elsewhere, copper's 1.4% pop against a softer gold tape fits the growth-not-fear read, ags and softs sold off broadly (OJ -4.5%, cocoa -1.8%), and upside energy risks — the Russian-oil tariff bill and tightening winter LNG — argue against chasing the crude break.
